title: Correlation and least-squares regression
subtitle: Do two quantities move together, and can one predict the other? Fit the line that makes the smallest total squared miss.

scatter.title: Scatter plots and correlation
scatter.body: Plot pairs (x, y). The correlation coefficient r = Sxy/√(Sxx·Syy) lies in [−1, 1]: +1 perfect rising line, −1 perfect falling, 0 no linear relation. For the default data r = 0.9; a falling line gives -1. Correlation is not causation, and r ignores curved patterns.

ls.title: The least-squares line
ls.body: Fit ŷ = a + bx by minimising Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². Solution: b = Sxy/Sxx and a = ȳ − b·x̄, so the line always passes through (x̄, ȳ). Here slope 0.9 and intercept 1.3. The residuals are the vertical gaps; squaring them punishes big misses.

r2.title: How good is the fit? R²
r2.body: R² = 1 − SSres/SStot is the fraction of the variation in y explained by x; for simple regression R² = r². This fit has R² = 0.81 — 81 % explained. A high R² does not prove the model is right: always look at the residual plot for curves or fan shapes.

pit.title: Pitfalls
pit.body:
• Extrapolation beyond the data range is unreliable.
  • Outliers with large leverage can tilt the line.
  • Non-linear patterns: transform (log y) or use a curve.
  • Confounders: ice-cream sales and drownings correlate because of summer.

mult.title: More than one predictor
mult.body: Multiple regression fits ŷ = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … by the same least-squares idea (solve the normal equations XᵀXb = Xᵀy — the Gaussian elimination of Numerical Methods). Gradient descent finds the same minimum iteratively, which is how machine-learning models are trained.

rank.title: Rank correlation
rank.body: Spearman’s ρ applies the correlation formula to the ranks: ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)), d = rank difference. It detects any monotone relationship and resists outliers. Two judges ranking five entries with Σd² = 4 give ρ = 1 − 24/120 = 0.8.
